title: Talking Animals: the Serpent and Balaam's Donkey
lead: Two animals speak in the Bible's stories: the snake in Eden, who talks the woman into eating from the forbidden tree (Genesis 3:1–5), and Balaam's donkey, whose mouth the LORD opens to rebuke her master (Numbers 22:28–30). One speaks to deceive, the other to tell the truth a prophet could not see. Readers have taken them as miracles, as visions or as the language of story, and Christians from the New Testament on have seen the devil behind the snake (Revelation 12:9).

sections.b: "Now the snake was shrewder than every wild animal of the field that the LORD God had made" (Genesis 3:1). The Hebrew nachash is the ordinary word for a snake, and Genesis calls it one of the animals God made. There is a word play: the man and woman were 'arummim, "naked" (Genesis 2:25), and the snake was 'arum, "shrewd." The snake's first words twist what God said: "Is it really true that God said, 'You must not eat from any tree of the garden'?" (Genesis 3:1). After the fall God curses it to crawl on its belly (Genesis 3:14). Genesis never names Satan. Later readers did: the Wisdom of Solomon says that through the devil's envy death came into the world (Wisdom of Solomon 2:24), and Revelation calls the dragon "the ancient serpent who is called the devil and Satan" (Revelation 12:9). Augustine wrote that the fallen angel "chose the serpent as his mouthpiece" (City of God 14.11). Josephus, retelling Genesis, says that in those days all the living creatures had one language, and that God took the serpent's speech away as part of its punishment (Jewish Antiquities, book 1, chapter 1).

sections.b: Balaam rides out to curse Israel. Three times his donkey sees the angel of the LORD with a drawn sword and turns aside, and three times Balaam beats her. "Then the LORD opened the donkey's mouth" (Numbers 22:28), and she asks why. Only then does the LORD uncover Balaam's eyes (Numbers 22:31). The famous seer is blind, and his donkey sees; the angel tells him he would have been killed, "and her I would have kept alive" (Numbers 22:33). 2 Peter recalls the scene: "a voiceless beast of burden, speaking out in a human voice, stopped the prophet's madness" (2 Peter 2:16). The Mishnah lists "the mouth of the donkey" among ten things God made at twilight on the eve of the first Sabbath (Mishnah Avot 5:6), that is, a wonder planned from creation.

sections.h: How to read a speaking animal
sections.b: As a miracle in history. Many Jewish and Christian readers have taken both scenes as events: God made the donkey speak, and the devil spoke through the snake, as 2 Peter, the Mishnah, Josephus and Augustine all assume. As a vision. Maimonides held that the speaking of Balaam's donkey happened in a prophetic vision, because an angel appears in the same account (Guide of the Perplexed 2:42). As the language of story. Many modern readers take the speaking snake as a feature of the kind of story Genesis 2–3 tells, and note that the Bible can use talking trees in a fable (Judges 9:8; 2 Kings 14:9) without claiming that trees talk. Whichever reading one takes, the two scenes make a matching point: speech belongs to God. The snake uses it to cast doubt on God's word; the donkey speaks only because "the LORD opened the donkey's mouth" (Numbers 22:28), and she speaks the truth.
